THE SECRET DOCTRINE

In 1853, the scholar known as Erard-Mollien read a paper before the Institute of France aiming to prove the antiquity of the Indian Zodiac. In its signs were found the root and philosophy of all the most important religious festivals of that country; the lecturer tried to demonstrate that the origin of these religious ceremonies goes back into the depths of time to at least 3,000 B.C. The Zodiac of the Hindus, he thought, was much older than the Zodiac of the Greeks and differed from it significantly in some details. In it, one sees the *Dragon* on a Tree, at the foot of which the Virgin, *Kanyâ-Durgâ*—one of the most ancient Goddesses—is placed on a Lion dragging the solar car. He said:

This is the reason why this Virgin Durgâ is not a simple *memento* of an astronomical fact, but truly the most ancient divinity of the Indian Olympus. She is evidently the same whose return was announced in all the Sibylline books—the source of Virgil's inspiration—an era of universal renewal. And why, since the months are still named according to this Indian Zodiac by the Malayâlam-speaking people [of southern India], should those people have abandoned it to adopt that of the Greeks? Everything proves, on the contrary, that these zodiacal figures were transmitted to the Greeks by the Chaldeans, who received them from the Brâhmans. <gloss>1</gloss>

But all this is very weak testimony. Let us, however, also remember what was said and accepted by the contemporaries of Volney, who remarks that since Aries was at its fifteenth degree in 1,447 B.C., it follows that the first degree of Libra could not have coincided with the vernal equinox later than 15,194 B.C. If we add to this, he argues, the 1,790 years that have passed since the birth of Christ, it appears that 16,984 years must have elapsed since the origin of the Zodiac. <gloss>2</gloss>

Dr. Schlegel, moreover, in his *Uranographie Chinoise*, assigns an antiquity of 18,000 years to the Chinese Astronomical Sphere. <gloss>3</gloss>

Nevertheless, since opinions quoted without adequate proof are of little use, it may be more useful to turn to scientific evidence. M. Bailly, the famous French astronomer of the last century, a member of the Academy, etc., asserts that the Hindu systems of astronomy are by far the oldest, and that the Egyptians, Greeks, Romans, and even the Jews derived their knowledge from them. In support of these views, he says:

The astronomers who preceded the era of 1491 are, first, the Alexandrian Greeks: Hipparchus, who flourished 125 years before our era, and Ptolemy, 260 years after Hipparchus. Following these were the Arabs, who revived the study of astronomy in the ninth century. These were succeeded by the Persians and the Tartars, to whom we owe the tables of Nassireddin in 1269 and those of Ulug-beg in 1437. Such is the succession of events in Asia as known before the Indian era of 1491. What, then, is

### THE ZODIAC AND ITS ANTIQUITY

...an epoch? It is the observation of the longitude of a star at a given moment—the place in the sky where it was seen—which serves as a point of reference, a starting point from which to calculate both the past and future positions of the star based on its observed motion. But an epoch is useless unless the motion of the star has been determined. A people new to science, forced to borrow a foreign astronomy, finds no difficulty in fixing an epoch, since the only observation needed is one that can be made at any moment. But what it needs above all, and what it is obliged to borrow, are those elements that depend on accurate determination and require continuous observation; above all, those motions which depend on time and which can only be accurately determined by centuries of observation. These motions, then, must be borrowed from a nation that has performed such observations and has centuries of labor behind it. We conclude, therefore, that a new people will not borrow the epochs of an ancient one without also borrowing their "average motions." Starting from this principle, we shall find that the Hindu epochs of 1491 and 3102 could not have been derived from those of either Ptolemy or Ulug-beg.

There remains the supposition that the Hindus, comparing their observations in 1491 with those previously made by Ulug-beg and Ptolemy, used the intervals between these observations to determine the average motions. The date of Ulug-beg is too recent for such a determination, while those of Ptolemy and Hipparchus were barely remote enough. But if the Hindu motions had been determined from these comparisons, the epochs would be connected together. Starting from the epochs of Ulug-beg and Ptolemy, we should arrive at all those of the Hindus. Hence, foreign epochs were either unknown or useless to the Hindus. <note>For a detailed scientific proof of this conclusion, see page 121 of M. Bailly's work, where the subject is discussed technically.</note>

We may add to this another important consideration. When a nation is obliged to borrow from its neighbors the methods or the average motions of its astronomical tables, it has an even greater need to borrow, besides these, the knowledge of the inequalities of the motions of the heavenly bodies, the motions of the apogee, of the nodes, and of the inclination of the ecliptic; in short, all those elements whose determination requires the art of observing, some instrumental appliances, and great industry. All these astronomical elements, differing more or less among the Greeks of Alexandria, the Arabs, the Persians, and the Tartars, exhibit no resemblance whatever to those of the Hindus. The latter, therefore, borrowed nothing from their neighbors.

If the Hindus did not borrow their epoch, they must have possessed a real one of their own, based on their own observations; and this must be either the epoch of the year 1491 AD or that of the year 3102 BC, the latter preceding the 1491 epoch by 4,592 years. We have to choose between these two epochs and decide which of them is based on observation. But before beginning the arguments that can and must decide the question, we may be permitted to make a few remarks to those who may be inclined to believe that modern observations and calculations have enabled the Hindus to determine the past positions of the heavenly bodies. It is far from easy to determine celestial movements with sufficient accuracy to ascend the stream of time for 4,592 years and to describe the phenomena that must have occurred at that period. Today, we possess excellent instruments; exact observations have been made for some two or three centuries, which already permit us to calculate the average motions of the planets with considerable accuracy; we have the observations of the Chaldeans, of Hipparchus, and of Ptolemy, which, owing to their remoteness from the present time, permit us to fix these motions with greater

certainty. Still, we cannot undertake to represent with invariable accuracy the observations throughout the long period intervening between the Chaldeans and ourselves, and still less can we undertake to determine with exactitude events occurring 4,592 years before our time. Cassini and Maier have each determined the secular motion of the moon, and they differ by 3 minutes and 43 seconds. This difference would give rise in forty-six centuries to an uncertainty of nearly three degrees in the moon’s position. No doubt one of these determinations is more accurate than the other; and it requires observations of very great antiquity to decide between them. But in very remote periods, where observations are lacking, it follows that we are uncertain as to the phenomena. How, then, could the Hindus have calculated back from the year 1491 A.D. to the year 3102 B.C. if they were only recent students of Astronomy?

The Orientals have never been what we are. However high an opinion of their knowledge we may form from the examination of their Astronomy, we cannot suppose them to have ever possessed that great array of instruments which distinguishes our modern observatories, and which is the product of simultaneous progress in various arts; nor could they have possessed that genius for discovery, which has hitherto seemed to belong exclusively to Europe, and which, taking the place of time, causes the rapid progress of science and human intelligence. If the Asiatics have been powerful, learned, and wise, it is power and time which have produced their merit and success of all kinds. Power has founded or destroyed their empires; now it has erected edifices imposing by their bulk, now it has reduced them to venerable ruins; and while these vicissitudes alternated with each other, patience accumulated knowledge, and prolonged experience produced wisdom. It is the antiquity of the nations of the East which has established their scientific fame.

If the Hindus possessed in 1491 a knowledge of the heavenly motions sufficiently accurate to enable them to calculate backwards for 4,592 years, it follows that they could only have obtained this knowledge from very ancient observations. To grant them such knowledge while refusing them the observations from which it is derived is to suppose an impossibility; it would be equivalent to assuming that at the outset of their career they had already reaped the harvest of time and experience. While on the other hand, if their epoch of 3102 is assumed to be real, it would follow that the Hindus had simply kept pace with successive centuries down to the year 1491 of our era. Thus, time itself was their teacher; they knew the motions of the heavenly bodies during these periods because they had seen them, and the duration of the Hindu people on earth is the cause of the fidelity of its records and the accuracy of its calculations.

It would seem that the problem as to which of the two epochs—3102 B.C. or 1491 A.D.—is the real one should be solved by one consideration: namely, that the ancients in general, and particularly the Hindus (as we may see by the arrangement of their Tables), calculated and therefore observed eclipses only. Now, there was no eclipse of the sun at the moment of the 1491 epoch, and no eclipse of the moon either fourteen days before or after that moment. Therefore, the 1491 epoch is not based on an observation. Regarding the epoch of 3102, the Brâhmans of Tirvaloor place it at sunrise on February 18th. The sun was then in the first point of the Zodiac according to its true longitude. Other Tables show that at the preceding midnight the moon was in the same place, but according to its average longitude. The Brâhmans also tell us that this first point, the origin of their Zodiac, was, in the year 3102, 54 degrees behind the equinox. It follows that the origin—the first point of their Zodiac—was therefore in the sixth degree of Aquarius.

There occurred, therefore, about this time and place an average conjunction; and indeed this conjunction is given in our best Tables: La Caille’s for the sun and

<margin>Maier's tables for the moon</margin> There was no eclipse of the sun, as the moon was too distant from her node; but fourteen days later, the moon, having approached the node, must have been eclipsed. Maier's tables, used without correction for acceleration, show this eclipse; but they place it during the day when it could not have been observed in India. Cassini's tables show it occurring at night, which demonstrates that Maier's motions are too rapid for distant centuries when acceleration is not accounted for; this also proves that, despite the improvement of our knowledge, we can still be uncertain about the actual aspect of the heavens in past times.

Therefore, we believe that, between the two Hindu epochs, the real one is the year 3102, because it was accompanied by an eclipse that could be observed, and which must have served to determine it. This is a first proof of the truth of the longitude assigned by the Hindus to the sun and the moon at this instant; and this proof would perhaps be sufficient, were it not that this ancient determination becomes of the greatest importance for the verification of the motions of these bodies, and must therefore be supported by every possible proof of its authenticity.

We notice, first, that the Hindus seem to have combined two epochs together into the year 3102. The Tirvaloor Brahmins reckon primarily from the first moment of the Kali Yuga, but they have a second epoch placed 2 days, 3 hours, 32 minutes, and 30 seconds later. The latter is the true astronomical epoch, while the former seems to be a civil era. But if this epoch of the Kali Yuga had no reality and was the mere result of a calculation, why should it be divided this way? Their calculated astronomical epoch would have become that of the Kali Yuga, which would have been placed at the conjunction of the sun and the moon, as is the case with the epochs of the three other Tables. They must have had some reason for distinguishing between the two, and this reason can only be due to the circumstances and the time of the epoch, which therefore could not be the result of calculation. This is not all; starting from the solar epoch determined by the rising of the sun on February 18th, 3102, and tracing back events 2 days, 3 hours, 32 minutes, and 30 seconds, we come to 2:27:30 a.m. on February 16th, which is the instant of the beginning of the Kali Yuga. It is curious that this age was not made to commence at one of the four great divisions of the day. It might be suspected that the epoch should be midnight, and that the 2 hours, 27 minutes, and 30 seconds are a meridian correction. But whatever the reason for fixing on this moment may have been, it is plain that were this epoch the result of calculation, it would have been just as easy to carry it back to midnight so as to make the epoch correspond to one of the chief divisions of the day, instead of placing it at a moment fixed by the fraction of a day.

Second, the Hindus assert that at the first moment of Kali Yuga there was a conjunction of all the planets, and their Tables show this conjunction, while ours indicate that it might actually have occurred. Jupiter and Mercury were in exactly the same degree of the ecliptic, with Mars being 8° and Saturn 17° distant from it. It follows that about this time, or some fifteen days after the commencement of Kali Yuga, and as the sun advanced in the Zodiac, the Hindus saw four planets emerge successively from the Sun's rays: first Saturn, then Mars, then Jupiter and Mercury; and these planets appeared united in a relatively small space. Although Venus was not among them, a fondness for the marvelous caused it to be called a general conjunction of all the planets. The testimony of the Brahmins here coincides with that of our Tables; and this evidence, the result of a tradition, must be founded on actual observation.

Third, we may remark that this phenomenon was visible about a fortnight after the epoch, and exactly at the time when the eclipse of the moon must have been observed, which served to fix the epoch. The two observations mutually confirm each other, and whoever made the one must have made the other also.

4th. We may also believe that the Hindus determined the position of the moon's node at the same time; this seems indicated by their calculation. They provide the longitude of this point of the lunar orbit for the time of their epoch, and to this they add 40 minutes as a constant, which is the node's motion over 12 days and 14 hours. It is as if they stated that this determination was made thirteen days after their epoch, and that to make it correspond to that epoch, we must add the 40 minutes through which the node retrograded in that interval. This observation is, therefore, from the same date as that of the lunar eclipse, thus providing three observations which confirm each other.

5th. It appears from the description of the Hindu Zodiac given by M. C. Gentil that the positions of the stars named the Eye of Taurus and the Wheat-ear of Virgo can be determined for the beginning of the *Kali Yuga*. Now, comparing these places with the actual positions, adjusted by our precession of the equinoxes to the moment in question, we see that the starting point of the Hindu Zodiac must lie between the fifth and sixth degree of Aquarius <note>1 Libra, in the 1888 edition, p. 663.</note>. The Brahmins, therefore, were right in placing it in the sixth degree of that sign, especially since this small difference may be due to the proper motion of the stars, which is unknown. Thus, it was yet another observation that guided the Hindus in this fairly accurate determination of the first point of their movable Zodiac.

It does not seem possible to doubt the existence of observations of this date in antiquity. The Persians say that four beautiful stars were placed as guardians at the four corners of the world. Now it happens that at the beginning of the *Kali Yuga*, 3,000 or 3,100 years before our era, the Eye of the Bull and the Heart of the Scorpion were exactly at the equinoctial points, while the Heart of the Lion and the Southern Fish were very near the solstitial points. An observation of the rising of the Pleiades in the evening, seven days before the autumnal equinox, also belongs to the year 3000 before our era. This and similar observations are collected in Ptolemy's calendars, though he does not give their authors; and these, which are older than those of the Chaldeans, may well be the work of the Hindus. They are well acquainted with the constellation of the Pleiades, and while we commonly call it the "*Poussinière*," they name it *Pillâlu-kodı* <note>2 This is a Tamil word.</note>—the "Hen and chickens." This name has, therefore, passed from people to people and comes to us from the most ancient nations of Asia. We see that the Hindus must have observed the rising of the Pleiades and used it to regulate their years and their months; for this constellation is also called *Krittikâ*. Now they have a month of the same name, and this coincidence can only be due to the fact that this month was announced by the rising or setting of the constellation in question.

But what is even more decisive in showing that the Hindus observed the stars, and in the same way that we do—marking their position by their longitude—is a fact mentioned by *Augustinus Riccius*: that according to observations attributed to *Hermes* and made 1,985 years before Ptolemy, the brilliant star in the Lyre and that in the heart of the Hydra were each seven degrees ahead of their respective positions as determined by Ptolemy. This determination seems very extraordinary. The stars move forward regularly with respect to the equinox; and Ptolemy should have found the longitudes to be 28 degrees greater than they were 1,985 years before his time. Besides, there is a remarkable peculiarity about this fact: the same error or difference is found in the positions of both stars; therefore, the error was due to some cause affecting both stars equally. It was to explain this peculiarity that the Arab *Thebith* imagined the stars had an oscillatory movement, causing them to advance and recede alternately. This hypothesis was easily disproved; but the observations attributed to

Hermes remained unexplained. Their explanation, however, is found in Hindu Astronomy. At the date fixed for these observations, 1,985 years before Ptolemy, the first point of the Hindu Zodiac was 35 degrees ahead of the equinox; therefore, the longitudes calculated for this point are 35 degrees more than those calculated from the equinox. But after the passage of 1,985 years, the stars would have advanced 28 degrees, and there would remain a difference of only 7 degrees between the longitudes of Hermes and those of Ptolemy. The difference would be the same for the two stars, since it is due to the difference between the starting points of the Hindu Zodiac and that of Ptolemy, which calculates from the equinox. This explanation is so simple and natural that it must be true. We do not know whether Hermes, so celebrated in antiquity, was a Hindu, but we see that the observations attributed to him are calculated in the Hindu manner, and we conclude that they were made by the Hindus. They, therefore, were able to make all the observations we have listed, and which we find noted in their Tables.

6. The observation of the year 3102, which seems to have fixed their era, was not a difficult one. We see that the Hindus, having once determined the moon's daily motion of 13º 10' 35", used it to divide the Zodiac into 27 constellations related to the period of the moon, which takes about 27 days to traverse it.

It was by this method that they determined the positions of the stars in this Zodiac; it was thus they found that a certain star of the Lyre was at 8$^s$ 24º, and the Heart of the Hydra was at 4$^s$ 7º—longitudes which are attributed to Hermes, but which are calculated on the Hindu Zodiac. Similarly, they discovered that the Wheat-ear of Virgo forms the beginning of their fifteenth constellation, and the Eye of Taurus the end of the fourth; these stars being at 6$^s$ 6º 40' and 1$^s$ 23º 20' of the Hindu Zodiac respectively. This being so, the eclipse of the moon which occurred fifteen days after the Kali Yuga epoch took place at a point between the Wheat-ear of Virgo and the star θ of the same constellation. These stars are approximately one constellation apart, one beginning the fifteenth and the other the sixteenth. Thus, it would not be difficult to determine the moon's place by measuring her distance from one of these stars; from these, they deduced the position of the sun, which is opposite to the moon. Then, knowing their average motions, they calculated that the moon was at the first point of the Zodiac according to her average longitude at midnight on the 17th-18th of February in the year 3102 before our era, and that the sun occupied the same place twelve hours later according to his true longitude—an event which fixes the beginning of the Hindu year.

7. The Hindus state that 20,400 years before the age of Kali Yuga, the first point of their Zodiac coincided with the vernal equinox, and that the sun and moon were in conjunction there. This epoch is obviously fictitious,<note>¹ Why it should be "fictitious" can never be made clear by European scientists.</note> but we may inquire from what point, and from what epoch, the Hindus set out in establishing it. Taking the Hindu values for the revolution of the sun and moon, namely, 365d 6h 12m 30s, and 27d 7h 43m 13s, we have:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20,400 | revolutions of the sun | = | 7,451,277d 2h |
| 272,724 | revolutions of the moon | = | 7,451,277d 7h |

Such is the result obtained by starting from the Kali Yuga epoch; and the assertion of the Hindus, that there was a conjunction at the time stated, is founded on their Tables. But if, using the same elements, we start from the era of the year 1491, or from another placed in the year 1282 (which we shall speak of later), there will always be a difference of almost one or two days. It is both just and natural, in verifying the Hindu calculations, to use those among their elements which give the same result as they had arrived at themselves, and to set out from that one among their epochs which—

8. The Tirvaloor Brâhmans give the moon’s motion as 7^s 2º 0' 1'' <note>7^s 2º 8' in the 1888 edition, p. 666.</note> on the movable Zodiac, and as 9^s 7º 45' 1'' relative to the equinox during a vast period of 1,600,984 days (or 4,386 years and 94 days). We believe this motion was determined by observation; and we must state at the outset that the length of this period makes it poorly suited for calculating mean motions.

In their astronomical calculations, the Hindus make use of periods of 248, 3,031, and 12,372 days; besides the fact that these periods—though much too short—do not share the drawbacks of the previous one, they contain a precise number of lunar revolutions relative to the moon's apogee. These are, in reality, mean motions. The great period of 1,600,984 days is not simply a total of accumulated revolutions; there is no specific reason it should consist of 1,600,984 days instead of 1,600,985. It appears that only observation could have determined the number of days and established the start and end of the period. This period ends on May 21, 1282 A.D., at 5:15:30 at Benares. The moon was then at its apogee, according to the Hindus, and its longitude was:

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| The moon was then at its apogee, according to the Hindus, and its longitude was . . | 7^s 13º 45' 1'' |
| Maier gives the longitude as ... | 7^s 13º 53' 48'' |
| And places the apogee at .. | 7^s 14º 6' 54'' |

The Brâhmans' determination of the moon’s position thus differs by only nine minutes from ours, and their determination of the apogee by only twenty-two minutes. It is very clear that they could only have achieved such agreement with our best tables and such precision in celestial positions through observation. If, then, observation determined the end of this period, there is every reason to believe it also determined its beginning. Consequently, this motion, determined directly from nature, would necessarily align closely with the actual motions of the celestial bodies.

In fact, the Hindu motion during this long period of 4,883 years does not differ by a single minute from that of Cassini, and it matches that of Maier as well. Thus, two peoples—the Hindus and the Europeans—located at opposite ends of the world and perhaps just as far apart in their social systems, have achieved identical results regarding the moon’s motions. Such a level of agreement would be unbelievable if it were not based on observation and the shared imitation of nature. We should note that the four Hindu tables are all copies of the same system of astronomy. It is undeniable that the Siamese tables existed by 1687, when they were brought from India by M. de la Loubère. At that time, the tables of Cassini and Maier did not yet exist; thus, the Hindus already possessed the exact motions contained in these tables while we did not yet have them. <note>The following is an answer to those scientists who might suspect that our astronomy was carried to India and communicated to the Hindus by our missionaries. 1. "...be seven cubits deep"—"cubits" standing here, of course, for divisions, zones, and principles. Therein, "in the great Mother, all the Gods and the Seven Great Ones are born." Both Fohat and Toom are addressed as the "Great Ones of the Seven Magic Forces" who "conquer the Serpent Apap," or Matter.<note>See *Book of the Dead*, cviii, 4</note>

No student of Occultism, however, should be misled by the typical phraseology used in the translations of Hermetic works into believing that the ancient Egyptians or Greeks spoke of and referred—like monks in every conversation—to a Supreme Being, God, the "One Father and Creator of all," and so on, in the way found on every page of such translations. That was not actually the case, and those texts are *not* the *original* Egyptian texts. They are Greek compilations, the earliest of which does not go beyond the early period of Neo-Platonism. No Hermetic work written by Egyptians—as we may see from the *Book of the Dead*—would speak of the one universal God of the monotheistic systems. The one *absolute* cause of all was as unnameable and unpronounceable in the mind of the ancient Egyptian philosopher as it is forever *unknowable* in the conception of Mr. Herbert Spencer. As for the Egyptians in general, as M. Maspero well remarks, whenever they arrived at the notion of divine unity, the "One God" was never simply "God." M. Lepage-Renouf very accurately observed that the word *Noutir Nouti*, "God," had never ceased to be a *generic name* to become a personal one.

Every God was the "one living and unique God" to them. Their monotheism was purely geographical. If the Egyptian of Memphis proclaimed the unity of Phtah to the exclusion of Ammon, the Egyptian of Thebes proclaimed the unity of Ammon to the exclusion of Phtah <note>As we now see done in India in the case of the Shaivas and the Vaishnavas.</note>. Ra, the "One God" at Heliopolis, is not the same as Osiris, the "One God" at Abydos, and can be worshipped side by side with him without being absorbed by him. The one God is but the God of the *nome* or the city, *Noutir Nouti*, and does not exclude the existence of the one God of the neighboring town or *nome*. In short, whenever we are speaking of Egyptian monotheism, we ought to speak of the "Gods-One" of Egypt, and not of the "One God."<note>Maspero in the *Guide au Musée de Boulaq*, p. 152 (1883)</note>

It is by this feature, preeminently Egyptian, that the authenticity of the various so-called *Hermetic Books* ought to be tested, and it is totally absent from the Greek fragments known under this name. This proves that a Greek Neo-Platonic, or perhaps a Christian hand, had a significant share in the editing of such works. Of course, the fundamental philosophy is there, and in many places, it is intact. But the style has been altered and smoothed in a monotheistic direction—as much as, if not more than, that of the Hebrew Genesis in its Greek and Latin translations. They may be *Hermetic works*, but they are not works written by either of the two Hermes—or rather, by Thot-Hermes, the directing...

<summary>The author argues that ancient Egyptian religion was not monotheistic in the modern sense but consisted of localized "One-Gods" specific to different regions. The text also claims that modern translations of Hermetic works have been edited by later Greek or Christian hands to appear more monotheistic than the original Egyptian sources.</summary>

...the Intelligence of the Universe<note>See *Book of the Dead*, xciv</note> or by Thoth, his terrestrial incarnation called Trismegistus, of the Rosetta stone.

But all is doubt, negation, iconoclasm, and brutal indifference in our age of a hundred “isms” and no religion. Every idol is broken except the Golden Calf.

Unfortunately, no nation or nations can escape their Karmic fate, any more than can units and individuals. History itself is dealt with by so-called historians as unscrupulously as legendary lore. For this, Augustin Thierry has made the *amende honorable* <note>A public apology or act of reparation</note>, if one may believe his biographers. He deplored the erroneous principle that made all *would-be* historiographers lose their way, and each presume to correct tradition—“that *vox-populi* [voice of the people] which nine times out of ten is *vox Dei* [voice of God]”—and he finally admitted that *real history rests in legend alone*, for he adds:

> Legend is living tradition, and three times out of four it is truer than what we call *History*<note>*Revue des Deux Mondes*, 1865, pp. 157-8</note>

While Materialists deny everything in the Universe except Matter, Archaeologists are trying to dwarf Antiquity and seek to destroy every claim of Ancient Wisdom by tampering with Chronology. Our present-day Orientalists and historical writers are to ancient History what white ants are to the buildings in India. More dangerous even than those termites, the modern Archaeologists—the “authorities” of the future in the matter of Universal History—are preparing for the history of past nations the fate of certain edifices in tropical countries. As Michelet said:

> History will tumble down and break into atoms in the lap of the twentieth century, devoured to its foundations by her annalists.

Very soon, indeed, under their combined efforts, it will share the fate of those ruined cities in both Americas, which lie deeply buried under impassable virgin forests. Historical facts will remain concealed from view by the inextricable jungles of modern hypotheses, denials, and skepticism. But very happily, *actual* History repeats herself, for she proceeds, like everything else, in cycles; and dead facts and events deliberately drowned in the sea of modern skepticism will ascend once more and reappear on the surface.

In Volumes 3 and 4, the very fact that a work with claims to Philosophy, which is also an exposition of the most abstruse problems, has to be commenced by tracing the evolution of mankind from what are regarded as supernatural beings—*Spirits*—will arouse the most malevolent criticism. Believers in, and the defenders of, the SECRET DOCTRINE, however, will have to

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This word should be Vyâhrritis, meaning "utterance." The three words—Bhûh, Bhuvah, and Svah (or Suvah)—are repeated by Brahmins when they perform the daily sandhyâ, which consists of worship and prayers.

*The Value of the Term Raven*, p 161
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Taking the value of $\pi$ as $\frac{355}{113}$, the circumference is taken as 355 and the diameter as 113. Now, if the circle is divided into six parts and each of these is subdivided by six, the circle will contain 355 $\times$ 6, or 2130 parts—that is, 213/0. Again, if the circle is divided by six diameters, or into twelve parts as described above, and these are divided by six, we will have 355 $\times$ 12, or 4260 parts, which is 426/0 or 213 $\times$ 2.

"*Is Light a Body or not?*" p 206
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Today, scientists would reply that light is ***both***.

*Sir Isaac Newton*, p 218, etc
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Full credit is now granted to Sir Isaac Newton for his "inspired guesses."

Section 4, p. 224
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Most of the scientific theories examined in this Section are now outdated.

Section 5, p 231
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The modern ideas presented in *The New Conceptions of Matter* by C. G. Darwin address this Section.
